question.text:
Given that $X\sim \chi^2(6),$ what is $P\left(X < 4\right)$ expressed as an integral?

Hint: The probability density function $\chi^2(k)$ is given by

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2^{k/2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{k}{2} \right) } x^{k/2 - 1} e^{-x/2}, & x \geq 0 \\[3pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
A chi-square random variable $X \sim \chi^2(k)$ with $k$ degrees of freedom has the following probability density function:

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2^{k/2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{k}{2} \right) } x^{k/2 - 1} e^{-x/2}, & x \geq 0 \\[3pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

We're given that $X\sim \chi^2(6).$ So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{8 \Gamma \left( 3 \right) } x^2 e^{-x/2}, & x \geq 0 \\[3pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

Recalling that $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$ for any natural number $n \geq 1,$ we have

\[ \Gamma(3) = 2! = 2. \]

So, the probability distribution becomes

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{16} x^2 e^{-x/2}, & x \geq 0 \\[3pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Finally, we express $P\left(X < 4\right)$ as follows:

\[\begin{align*} P\left(X < 4\right) &= \int_0^{4} f(x) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{4} \dfrac{1}{16} x^2 e^{-x/2} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{16} \int_0^{4} x^2 e^{-x/2} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] \end{align*}\]

Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:

\[ \int_0^{9} x e^{-x/2} \, \textrm dx \approx 3.75560 \]

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2^{k/2} \Gamma \left( \dfrac{k}{2} \right) } x^{k/2 - 1} e^{-x/2}, & x \geq 0 \\[3pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

We're given that $X\sim \chi^2(4).$ So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{4 \Gamma \left( 2\right) } x e^{-x/2}, & x \geq 0 \\[3pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Probability Involving Sums of Squared Standard Normal Variables

question.text:
Let the random variable $Y$ be defined as \[ Y = Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{10}^2 \] where $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ for $1\leq i\leq 10.$ Find the value $y$ such that $P(Y\geq y) = 0.01.$

Hint: The table below gives the values of $x$ that satisfy $P(X\geq x) = p,$ where $X\sim \chi^2(k).$

$k \setminus p$ $0.010$ $0.050$ $0.100$ $0.150$ $0.200$
$ 9 $ $\,21.666\,$ $\,16.919\,$ $\,14.684\,$ $\,13.288\,$ $\,12.242\,$
$ 10 $ $\,23.209\,$ $\,18.307\,$ $\,15.987\,$ $\,14.534\,$ $\,13.442\,$
$ 11 $ $\,24.725\,$ $\,19.675\,$ $\,17.275\,$ $\,15.767\,$ $\,14.631\,$
question.explanation:
If $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ for $1\leq i \leq k$ are independent normal random variables, then the sum \[ Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{k}^2 \] follows a $\chi^2(k)$ distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom.

So, in our case, we have

\[ Y = Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{10}^2 \sim \chi^2(10). \]

We wish to find the value $y$ such that $P(Y\geq y) = 0.01$ This can be found from the given table:

$k \setminus p$ $0.010$ $0.050$ $0.100$ $0.150$ $0.200$
$ 9 $ $\,21.666\,$ $\,16.919\,$ $\,14.684\,$ $\,13.288\,$ $\,12.242\,$
$ 10 $ $\,\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{23.209}\,$ $\,18.307\,$ $\,15.987\,$ $\,14.534\,$ $\,13.442\,$
$ 11 $ $\,24.725\,$ $\,19.675\,$ $\,17.275\,$ $\,15.767\,$ $\,14.631\,$

So, we have

\[ P(Y\geq 23.209) = 0.01. \]

Therefore, $y=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{23.209}.$
